The CLI is already a useful portable foundation. The main dependencies on Claude are in hook packaging, session summarization, and the instructions. I also found conflicting retrieval guidance: the skill recommends three different starting points. I’m checking the actual behavior so the recommendations address more than wording.

The existing checks pass: TypeScript validation and all 386 tests. They don’t yet measure agent task performance, though. I found two concrete portability gaps: overriding the summarizer still forces Claude’s `-p --model haiku` arguments, and the transcript reader only recognizes one event format. I’m testing those with isolated fixtures.

The probes confirmed a silent failure: a Codex-style transcript reached the summarizer with none of its conversation text, yet the result reported `degraded: false`. A separate read returned over 100 KB despite the bounded-retrieval positioning. These make transcript validation and consistent output limits higher priorities than prompt tuning.

**I’d make KB a portable CLI with a thin skill and optional harness adapters.** Any agent with shell and file access should get the complete workflow; hooks should add convenience.

The existing foundation is useful: Markdown storage, source attribution, structured retrieval, and caching. I ran `bun run lint && bun run test`: **386 tests passed**. Isolated probes still exposed important gaps.

I’d prioritize these changes:

| Priority | Finding | Improvement |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Prevent silent knowledge loss** | A synthetic Codex-style transcript produced empty excerpts. Summarization received no conversation text but reported `degraded: false`. [Source](/Users/justinbeaudry/Projects/kb/src/lib/summarizer.ts:201) | Normalize transcripts into a documented event format. Validate recognized turns, preserve provenance, and explicitly reject unsupported formats. |
| **2. Bound context everywhere** | This session’s startup injection was 931 lines, approximately 7,865 tokens. A `kb get` probe returned over 100 KB. [Source](/Users/justinbeaudry/Projects/kb/src/commands/get.ts:66) | Make lazy startup the canonical behavior, provide migration for existing vaults, and add consistent byte limits, range selection, and continuation information to retrieval commands. |
| **3. Remove provider assumptions** | `KB_SUMMARIZE_COMMAND` changes the executable but still appends `-p --model haiku`. [Source](/Users/justinbeaudry/Projects/kb/src/lib/summarizer.ts:331) | Define a provider-neutral stdin/stdout contract with configurable arguments, deadlines, and validated output. Also support summaries supplied by the active agent. |
| **4. Eliminate conflicting instructions** | The skill recommends topic-first, map-first, and qmd-first retrieval. Querying also instructs agents to save novel knowledge automatically, while another rule requires confirmation. [Source](/Users/justinbeaudry/Projects/kb/skills/kb/SKILL.md:77) | Establish one retrieval decision tree. Keep queries from changing curated knowledge. Route ingestion through the user’s authorized scope. |
| **5. Measure agent outcomes** | Skill-contract tests check whether instruction strings exist. They cannot establish whether agents retrieve the right evidence or follow the workflow. [Tests](/Users/justinbeaudry/Projects/kb/tests/skill-contract.test.ts:8) | Add task evaluations that inspect answers, citations, tool usage, and resulting vault changes. |

For portability, I’d establish three clear boundaries:

- **The skill teaches decisions.** When to retrieve, how to select evidence, when evidence is insufficient, and when to propose a knowledge update. Use the standard `SKILL.md` format, explicit shell/file requirements, and task-specific references loaded on demand. That matches the [Agent Skills specification](https://agentskills.io/specification).
- **The CLI handles mechanics.** Vault discovery, validation, search, bounded reads, backlink calculation, and operational logging. Add consistent JSON output and machine-readable errors. Extend `doctor` to report the resolved vault, version, and available capabilities.
- **Adapters handle harness details.** Hook event names, transcript conversion, installation locations, and native permission integration. Every essential operation also needs an explicit CLI path when hooks are unavailable.

I’d also simplify the skill itself:

- Replace generic “persistent memory” positioning with concrete triggers: recalling previous decisions, finding project knowledge, ingesting sources, and maintaining the vault.
- Move page templates and maintenance details out of the query path. The main skill currently requires reading `KB.md`, whose template adds another 439 lines.
- Keep qmd behind KB’s retrieval interface, so agents use the same workflow regardless of available MCP tool names.
- Replace “touch 5–15 pages” and mandatory link counts with relevance-based updates. Those instructions can encourage unnecessary edits and weak connections.
- Add a few worked examples covering a successful lookup, conflicting evidence, and no useful result.
- Describe all retrieved content as evidence, never executable instructions. Document host-specific protections accurately.

These choices should reduce ambiguous tool selection and unnecessary context, consistent with [Anthropic’s tool-design guidance](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents).

**“Best-in-class” should become a measured target.** Start with roughly 20 realistic tasks covering exact recall, paraphrased queries, superseded decisions, absent evidence, duplicate ingestion, interrupted extraction, and unsupported transcripts.

Compare plain Markdown search, current KB, and the revised version across multiple harnesses, including a shell-only setup. Hold model and task conditions constant within each comparison. Measure:

- Task success and citation correctness.
- Unsupported claims and unintended knowledge changes.
- Tokens, tool calls, latency, and cost per successful task.
- Reliability across repeated runs.
- Skill activation on relevant requests and restraint on unrelated requests.

Use held-out tasks and inspect actual vault changes, following [outcome-based agent evaluation](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents).

My recommended first increment is **a baseline evaluation, transcript validation, consistent retrieval limits, and one coherent query workflow**. Those address demonstrated failures and give us evidence for subsequent optimization. The repository is unchanged.

name: task-graph
description: Use when starting any non-trivial task — multi-step work, changes touching 2+ files, research or content jobs with several parts, or anything that would otherwise become one long session. Runs the task as a graph of bounded nodes (subagents) with gates, correction/learning edges, and graph.md / checks.md / progress.md so another session can rerun, resume, or extend it. Also triggers on "run this as a graph", "agent graph", "split this into nodes", or resuming a directory that already has graph.md + progress.md. Skip for trivial changes (typo, rename, single-line fix).
---

# Task Graph

Adapted from @hanakoxbt's Karpathy-inspired graph prompt (inspired by
github.com/karpathy/autoresearch; graph adaptation from agent-layers.vercel.app).
Not written or endorsed by Andrej Karpathy.

## Goal

Complete the task as a graph of bounded nodes, not one long session. Leave a
usable result, a verification report, and `graph.md` so another session can
rerun or extend it. Define completion before starting. Stop when every node's
checks pass or the agreed limit is reached.

## Role

Act as the lead that designs, runs, and maintains this graph. Read the existing
project instructions (AGENTS.md / AGENTS.md) and inspect current work before
editing. Plan and merge yourself; give bounded work to subagents. Record
decisions that change the graph.

## Principles

Adapted from Karpathy's autoresearch:
- Establish a baseline before changing the system.
- Give every node one clear scope and a fixed evaluator.
- Change one thing, measure it, and keep useful improvements. Record failed attempts too.
- Prefer fewer nodes when results are comparable.

## Inputs

Fill these before starting:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| TASK | What is being done |
| OUTPUT | Deliverable and output path |
| CHECKS | Acceptance checks |
| SOURCES | Source material |
| SCOPE | Allowed changes (paths, systems) |
| LIMIT | Run limit (attempts, nodes, time, or spend) |

Infer what you can from the request and repo. If a missing detail changes the
outcome, ask **one** focused question. Record the filled inputs at the top of
`graph.md`.

Artifacts (`graph.md`, `checks.md`, `progress.md`) live in the project's
planning directory if one exists (e.g. `docs/plans/<task-slug>/`), otherwise
`.graph/<task-slug>/` at the repo root.

## Layer 1 — Split

Break the task into nodes before any work starts. A node is one bounded job:
one input, one output, one check.
- Split by what each node must read, not by folder.
- Draw an edge only when a node consumes another node's output.
- Mark nodes with no edge between them as parallel.

Write nodes, edges, and checks into `graph.md` and **pause for approval**.

`graph.md` shape:

```markdown
# Graph: <task>
## Inputs
TASK / OUTPUT / CHECKS / SOURCES / SCOPE / LIMIT
## Nodes
| id | kind (model/code) | reads | writes | check | depends on |
## Parallel groups
## Code nodes
## Rules learned
## Decisions log
```

## Layer 2 — Nodes

Run each node as its own subagent (Agent tool) with only the context it needs:
1. Pass the node spec, its inputs, and its check.
2. Build the artifact for that node only.
3. Run the node's check against the saved artifact.
4. Return the output path, verdict, and evidence.

Keep node specs reusable across new source sets. Dispatch independent nodes in
a single message so they run concurrently.

## Layer 3 — Code nodes

If a step has exactly one correct answer (merge, sort, dedupe, compare, count,
lint, test, build), do it as code, not as a model call. A model call is for
judgment only.
- List every code node in `graph.md`.
- Never route a deterministic step through a subagent.

If a required tool is unavailable, name the blocker and preserve the nodes that
can still be completed.

## Layer 4 — Permissions

Check the active permissions before running the graph. Keep edits inside SCOPE.
Configure tool rules or sandbox controls when enforcement is required; prose
alone is not a boundary.
- Ask before publishing, sending, or spending.
- Never let two nodes edit the same file (use worktree isolation if needed).
- Preserve a recoverable version (commit, branch, or copy) before risky merges.

## Layer 5 — Gates

Put a gate on every edge that carries risky work. Open it on evidence, in this
order: deterministic checks first, then the node's report, the model's
confidence last.

Save `checks.md` with a row for each requirement:

```markdown
| node | requirement | verdict | evidence |
```

Verdict is `pass`, `fail`, or `unresolved`. Include file paths or actual check
output. Leave missing evidence visible.

## Layer 6 — Return paths

- **Correction edge:** a failed gate sends the unit back to the node that made
  it, with the reason, the evidence, and the scope "fix this node only". Cap at
  three attempts.
- **Learning edge:** after an accepted result, write the rule it proves into
  `graph.md` (Rules learned) so the next run starts from it.

## Layer 7 — Completion

Before execution, write a completion checklist from CHECKS. Each item must point
to observable evidence:
- Every node's output exists and can be opened.
- Every gate ran against the saved version.
- Failures are fixed or explicitly reported.
- `graph.md` matches the nodes that actually ran.

If a limit or blocker stops the run, return a partial status with the exact
nodes left.

## Execution loop

1. Read `graph.md` and pick the next ready nodes.
2. Run independent nodes in parallel.
3. Pass every output through its gate.
4. Return failed units, never the whole batch.
5. Merge accepted outputs in code.
6. Continue until completion, a blocker, or LIMIT.

Do not weaken a gate to obtain a pass.

## Handoff

After each stage, update `progress.md`:
- **Graph:** nodes done, running, and blocked.
- **Outputs:** exact paths to the current saved files.
- **Decisions:** what changed in `graph.md` and why.
- **Open issues:** failures, uncertainties, and blockers.
- **Next action:** the next ready node.

On resumption, read `graph.md` and `progress.md` first, then continue from the
recorded next node.

## Delivery

Return OUTPUT, `graph.md`, `checks.md`, and `progress.md`. State what was
checked, what passed, and what remains unresolved. Save the graph as a reusable
template after review. Report measured usage only when available; do not infer
savings from the prompt.

## Fit with the standard workflow

- This skill is the execution shape; it doesn't replace project gates. Every
  code node set includes the stack's verification command from AGENTS.md
  (`bun run lint && bun run test`, `go vet ./... && go test -race ./... &&
  golangci-lint run`, `uv run ruff check . && uv run mypy . && uv run pytest`).
- When `ce-plan` produces a plan, Layer 1 turns its units into nodes; the
  approval pause covers both.
- TDD nodes: the "write failing test" node's check is that the test fails; the
  implementation node's check is that it passes.

</skill>

I’m using task-graph to organize the work. I’ll treat your “Go” as approval for the first increment we discussed: baseline evaluations, transcript validation, consistent retrieval limits, and one coherent query workflow. I’ll record the graph, then implement and verify each part.

The graph has three independent workstreams: transcript and summarizer portability, retrieval limits, and portable instructions with evaluations. Each will get a review gate before integration. I’m also using the Superpowers planning and TDD guidance, with task-graph as the execution workflow you requested.
